Constellation · Concept
Summary

The improvement loop is open. Constellation closes it.

School improvement runs on a loop most schools never close. Atlas tells a school where it stands in the national system. Lens tells it what it has been, honestly, through its own evidence. Orbit sets where it is going. And then the loop breaks, because nothing tells the school, while it still matters, whether any of it is working for actual children.

Constellation is the fourth instrument of the Institute platform: the live feedback loop. Leaders upload the data the school already produces, in whatever state it arrives: trip registers, intervention logs, assessment trackers, scanned evaluation forms, free-text notes. Constellation reads it, matches it to pupils, files it against the Orbit plan, and keeps one living picture: every pupil on one map, positioned by level of concern, coloured by direction of travel. It then reports back into Orbit, objective by objective, on whether the school's actions are making a measurable difference.

Three things separate it from every dashboard a school has been sold. It accepts real data rather than demanding clean data. It reads at the level of the individual child and finds the groups the averages hide. And it is honest: where an action is having no detectable effect, it says so, because a feedback loop that only flatters is worthless.

All screenshots in this paper come from the working prototype, running on modelled data. Every pupil shown is simulated.

The concept at a glance
1map

Every pupil on one School View: distance from the centre is level of concern, colour is direction of travel. The whole school in a glance; one child in a click.

4stages

Read, Understand, Place, Connect: any document, however untidy, becomes pupil-level evidence filed against the improvement plan, with every assumption logged.

5measures

Attendance, progress and engagement describe the pupil; enrichment and interventions describe the school's response. The two are never averaged together.

3verdicts

Each Orbit objective receives a plain answer each term: working, partly, or not yet, evidenced by matched-pupil comparisons and written back into the plan.

The instrument

What it could look like, and how it would work

Methodology · I

How messy data becomes evidence

One principle sits under everything: the AI reads, the maths counts. Language models are used to understand documents: what a file is, whose names are in it, what its columns mean. They are never used to do arithmetic, compute scores or invent numbers.

Every document goes through the same four stages. Read: proper parsers pull the raw content out of each file type, tables out of Excel, text out of Word, OCR for scans. Understand: the AI classifies the document (trip register, assessment tracker, intervention log, attendance export, CPD evaluation), identifies the period and cohort, and works out what each column means, whatever the school called it; everything inferred rather than read is logged as an assumption, and deterministic checks verify what they can. Place: every pupil mentioned is matched against the school roll. Connect: the evidence is filed against the Orbit strategy that expects it, the statistics are recomputed in code, and the School View updates.

The architecture rests on a spine: the school's MIS export is ground truth. The roll, with UPNs, is the one version of the truth, and every other document attaches to it or waits until it can. Matching runs strongest rule first: exact UPN; then full name and date of birth; then name with reg group; then fuzzy matching, which is never trusted alone.

Below the confidence threshold, Constellation asks a human instead of guessing. A wrong guess about which child did what is the one error a school will never forgive, so it is the one error the system is not allowed to make.

Each fact that survives becomes one tidy row: pupil, date, measure, value, source document, confidence. Evidence only accumulates, never overwrites, and confidence travels with it all the way up to the map.

Methodology · II

Five measures, in two families

Three measures describe how the pupil is doing; two describe what the school is doing about it. They answer different questions, so they are scored differently and never averaged together.

Table 1 · The five measures
MeasureFamilyThe question it answersComposition
AttendanceOutcomeIs this pupil here?Level vs expectation 50% · four-week trend 30% · pattern risk 20%
ProgressOutcomeIs this pupil learning at the rate they should?Quintile gap, prior vs current 60% · direction of travel 40%
EngagementOutcomeIs this pupil taking part in the life of the school?Praise-to-sanction ratio 40% · completion 30% · participation 30%
EnrichmentProvisionHas the school given this pupil what it promised everyone?Entitlement coverage, with breadth and recency
InterventionsProvisionIs the school giving this pupil the extra help their data suggests?Coverage × dosage; response deliberately scored elsewhere

A low outcome score is a concern about the pupil. A low provision score is a fact about the school: nobody took this child on a trip. Crossing the two produces the instrument's most important flag: declining outcomes plus empty provision.

Progress: quintiles, not flightpaths

Every pupil's prior attainment places them in a quintile of their own cohort; every assessment they sit is converted to a within-cohort percentile; the percentiles are averaged across assessments and quintiled the same way. Progress is the gap between the two quintiles: on the diagonal, performing in line with your start; below it, fallen behind; above it, exceeding. Because everything is ranked within the cohort, it does not matter that one test was out of 60 and another was brutal. The score beneath is computed on percentiles, so near-identical pupils are never split by a quintile boundary: quintiles for humans, percentiles for the maths.

Methodology · III

The concern score, and the promise behind it

A pupil's position on the map blends the outcome measures: progress 40%, attendance 40%, engagement 20%. Direction comes from each measure's own trend and sets the colour. And the blend carries one non-negotiable rule.

No compensation

A pupil collapsing in one core measure can never be averaged back to “on track” by strength elsewhere. Whatever the weighted blend says, the final band is capped at one band above the worst of attendance and progress. Consider the child every averaging system misses: bright, engaged, grades holding, attendance in serious trouble. The blend would call them “on track”; the cap holds them at “some concern”, so they stay visible. Averages are how schools lose children; this rule is how Constellation refuses to.

01 · The evidence ledger

Every document is listed with what it was read as, how many pupils matched, the confidence, and any assumption made. The numbers are defensible because their provenance is visible.

02 · The review queue

Ambiguous pupil matches, illegible scan pages and odd-looking values wait for a human answer rather than being guessed, and each answer teaches the matcher for next time.

03 · Traceability in under a minute

Any number on the screen can be traced back to a named document, a date and the assumptions made along the way. If a figure cannot survive that walk backwards, it does not belong on the map.

04 · The school's own data, joined up

Pupils are pseudonymised on shared views, all processing happens within the school's own account, and Constellation holds nothing the school did not already hold. It only joins it up.
